candidates.attacker_control: An attacker who can write a binary property (or a job/event resource binary property) in the JCR repository controls the serialized byte stream that is later passed to ObjectInputStream.readObject(). In addition, any application code that calls ValueMap.get(name, Serializable.class) / get(name, ObjectInputStream.class) on repository content feeds attacker-stored bytes into this sink. Sling's own eventing code does this automatically for binary properties of job resources (ResourceHelper.cloneValueMap, used for jobs under /var/eventing) and UpgradeTask reads 'slingevent:properties' through an ObjectInputStream, so the attacker does not need to control the calling code if one of these paths is triggered.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The deserialization of Serializable values is an intentional, documented feature (JcrNodeResource javadoc mentions 'loading serialized objects'; HelperData.getDynamicClassLoader supplies the loader), and Sling's own tests (JcrModifiablePropertyMapTest.testSerializable, JcrModifiableValueMapTest) round-trip an ArrayList through a binary property, so the code path is expected to exist and a fix would need an allow-list rather than outright removal. Prerequisites (write access, a Serializable-typed read, a gadget) are non-trivial; if the dynamic class loader is null, resolveClass falls back to the parent/context class loader, which still permits JDK gadget classes. The parameter flow from an HTTP request to the binary property write is application-specific and was not traced end-to-end; the automatic eventing trigger is limited to resources the eventing system reads.
candidates.impact: Unsafe deserialization of repository-controlled bytes: attacker-chosen classes are resolved and their readObject() logic executed inside the Sling JVM. With a suitable gadget on the class path this is arbitrary code execution (or at minimum arbitrary class instantiation and data corruption), potentially under Sling's eventing/service-user context rather than the attacker's own privileges, i.e. a privilege boundary crossing. Jobs/events run asynchronously with broad repository access, so a stored payload can be triggered automatically by normal processing.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Write access to the JCR resource/property whose binary value is later read as Serializable/ObjectInputStream (or an Sling event/job flow that copies attacker-controlled binary data into such a property). (2) A trigger that requests a Serializable/ObjectInputStream type for that property (Sling eventing cloneValueMap does so for every binary property of a job resource; UpgradeTask does so once for the job-properties blob; third-party/script code may also do so). (3) At least one gadget class reachable by the dynamic class loader or the thread-context class loader (JDK classes are loadable even when the dynamic class loader is absent).
candidates.root_cause: JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry.convertToType() treats a JCR binary (InputStream) property as serialized Java data and instantiates a custom ObjectInputStream that resolves any class name through the (optional) dynamic class loader, without any allow-list, type filter, or sandbox. PropertyObjectInputStream.resolveClass() simply returns classloader.loadClass(classDesc.getName()) for arbitrary names, so gadget classes are resolved and their readObject() logic executed during ois.readObject().
candidates.title: Unrestricted Java deserialization of repository binary property values in Sling JCR Resource (JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry)
candidates.trace: Repository binary property -> JcrPropertyMap.get(key, Serializable.class) (bundles/jcr/resource/.../JcrPropertyMap.java:137, also JcrValueMap.java:105 and JcrModifiableValueMap.java:104) -> JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry.convertToType(type,node,dynamicClassLoader) -> value instanceof InputStream and Serializable.isAssignableFrom(type) branch (JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry.java:326-330) -> new PropertyObjectInputStream(value, dynamicClassLoader).readObject() -> PropertyObjectInputStream.resolveClass() -> classloader.loadClass(arbitrary class name) (JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry.java:431-438) -> gadget class deserialized/executed. Automatic reachability: bundles/extensions/event ResourceHelper.cloneValueMap() obtains the ValueMap and calls vm.get(entry.getKey(), Serializable.class) for each InputStream-valued property (lines 203-206); UpgradeTask reads 'slingevent:properties' as ObjectInputStream (lines 202-215); the DEA ResourceHelper uses the same pattern (lines 43-58).
candidates.unverified: No runtime/exploit test was executed; no serialized payload or gadget chain was constructed. It is not verified whether this exact file is the target of the VUL4J-23 fix (the dataset metadata/ground truth is outside this review), nor whether every deployment exposes a code path that reads an attacker-writable binary property as Serializable. Reachability through the eventing JobManager requires a binary property in a processed job resource; the HTTP path that would plant such a property was not demonstrated.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (unsafe Java deserialization; missing class allow-list)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 6,303 model-visible files (source_root_files 6,304; 1 sensitive-named file excluded; no symlinks; no binaries read). The P1 relation index reports partial coverage: 4,904 Java files parsed, 718 files omitted/unparsed, 7 parse errors, 55,977 symbols, syntactic call/containment/inheritance candidates only, with control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution 'not implemented' — so index facts were used only to navigate and every candidate was verified against source text. I reviewed in depth: bundles/api (ResourceUtil, ResponseUtil, HtmlResponse), bundles/engine (DefaultErrorHandler, parameters, RequestHistoryConsolePlugin), bundles/servlets/get (all renderer servlets + RedirectServlet), bundles/servlets/post (SlingPostServlet, HtmlResponse, AbstractCreateOperation, NodeNameFilter, property handlers), bundles/servlets/resolver (ScriptResource), bundles/resourceresolver (URI helper, MapEntries aliases/vanity paths), bundles/jcr/resource (ValueMap/PropertyMap/PropertyMapCacheEntry/JcrResourceProvider), bundles/jcr/base and contentloader XML handling, bundles/auth core/form (redirect validation, TokenStore), bundles/extensions/xss (filter/validators), healthcheck core (servlet, serializers, tests), event/dea (ResourceHelper, UpgradeTask), feature-flags, i18n, explorer, discovery packaging; plus module/pom and provisioning files to date the tree. Not exhaustively reviewed: large parts of bundles/** (scripting, models, settings, installer, webdav/DAVEx, repoinit, resourceaccesssecurity), all of contrib/**, launchpad/**, testing/**, tooling/**, samples/**, and most JavaScript/JSP resources; these areas were only spot-checked or not inspected, so absence of an index record there is not coverage.
limitations: No code, build, test or scanner was executed; findings are static source observations, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.

The P1 relation index is syntactic only (no data-flow, control-flow or semantic resolution) and covers 4,904 of ~6,303 files; unreported areas were not reviewed merely because the index lacks records.

Exact snapshot dating/version mapping of the fix is uncertain: module versions (e.g. org.apache.sling.api 2.14.1-SNAPSHOT, org.apache.sling.jcr.resource 2.8.1-SNAPSHOT, org.apache.sling.engine 2.5.1-SNAPSHOT) are consistent with a pre-fix trunk state, but I could not determine the exact release in which an allow-list was introduced.

I could not verify whether VUL4J-23's ground-truth fix corresponds to this JCR Resource deserialization path, to the unescaped HtmlRendererServlet output, or to another issue; no dataset metadata, patches, CVEs or external data were consulted (and were out of scope for this run).

The attacker-controlled write path that plants a serialized binary property into a resource processed by the eventing code is application/repository-permission dependent and was not demonstrated end-to-end.
The relation index's security_call categories (deserialization/output/redirect/sql_or_process/process) are name-based navigation hints and were treated as non-authoritative.

rejected_leads.lead: HtmlRendererServlet writes resource path, sling:resourceType/super type and property names/values into HTML without escaping (bundles/servlets/get/src/main/java/org/apache/sling/servlets/get/impl/helpers/HtmlRendererServlet.java lines 103-162), while only the metadata field is escaped with StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml. This is a plausible stored-XSS sink (a content author can store markup in a node name/property; the .html dump of the default GET servlet would emit it unescaped).
rejected_leads.reason: Strong source evidence of missing encoding, but it requires repository write access plus a victim viewing the resource dump, and I could not confirm in-source that this exact escaping gap is the snapshot's fix target (no counterevidence file, no fix marker). Kept as an unconfirmed alternative rather than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HealthCheck JSONP callback reflection: HealthCheckExecutorServlet takes the raw 'callback' request parameter (line 234) and ResultJsonSerializer concatenates it into an application/javascript response (line 67) with no validation, allowing script injection via a crafted JSONP URL.
rejected_leads.reason: Genuine missing validation, but the servlet is registered through the OSGi HttpService at the configurable /system/health path (default chosen specifically so it is not internet-exposed), which lowers the default exposure and impact compared with the selected candidate; no evidence of a fix commit was found.

rejected_leads.lead: Feature flags accepted from request parameters: ConfiguredFeature.isEnabled() returns true whenever the request contains a matching 'feature' parameter (bundles/extensions/feature-flags/.../ConfiguredFeature.java lines 90-106).
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to be intentional test/override behavior (it can only force-enable, not disable), and no security gate in this snapshot was found to rely on these flags; not a defensible vulnerability on the available source evidence alone.

rejected_leads.lead: JsonQueryServlet executes the caller-supplied 'statement' via ResourceResolver.findResources (bundles/servlets/compat/.../JsonQueryServlet.java).
rejected_leads.reason: Intended query API; queries execute with the caller's JCR session and are subject to repository access control, so no privilege escalation or missing trust boundary was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Other ObjectInputStream uses (settings service, installer, distribution) and JDBC/JNDI-style calls flagged by the relation index.
rejected_leads.reason: These read local files, OSGi persistent state or cluster-internal packages rather than remotely supplied data; no attacker-controlled path was traced, so they were rejected as unconfirmed.
Values come from server-side info providers (JVM/system data), not from request input or writable content; no attacker control found.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Sling source snapshot (6,303 visible files; ~4,904 Java files parsed by the P1 index) as a defensive source review, focusing on unauthenticated/remote-reachable servlets, request-parameter handling, output encoding, and deserialization sinks. Across the tree the clearest concrete flaw I could verify in source is an unrestricted Java deserialization path in Sling JCR Resource: `JcrPropertyMapCacheEntry.convertToType()` deserializes repository binary property data with `ObjectInputStream` whose `resolveClass()` delegates to the Sling dynamic class loader for *any* class name, with no allow-list. This sink is reachable through the public `ValueMap.get(name, Serializable.class)/ObjectInputStream.class` API (JcrPropertyMap / JcrValueMap / JcrModifiableValueMap) and is exercised automatically by Sling's own eventing code (`ResourceHelper.cloneValueMap` calls `vm.get(key, Serializable.class)` for every binary property of a job resource; `UpgradeTask` reads `slingevent:properties` via `ObjectInputStream`). The expected impact is arbitrary class instantiation / potential remote code execution by a user who can store a serialized payload in a property that is later read as Serializable. I am submitting this as a single lead (not a confirmed vulnerability); strong alternative XSS leads exist in the same snapshot but were not selected because their exploitability/impact is lower or their exposure is more conditional. No code was executed and no runtime confirmation was performed.
